tagline.text: Forested mountains of the Bataan Peninsula, with the Mount Natib caldera and Pasukulan Falls

location.label: Location
location.text: Mountainous interior of the northern Bataan Peninsula, spanning six municipalities including Orani, Abucay, Morong and Bagac, and Balanga City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–3,000 (per person, transport, guide and registration)

children.text: Bataan National Park is a mountain forest in the northern interior of the Bataan Peninsula, covering about 23,688 hectares, with the Mount Natib caldera, waterfalls and valleys. The signature trips are the climb of Mount Natib, about 1,287 m above sea level, and the trek to the 60 m Pasukulan Falls, and both call for a guide.

Bataan National Park (also called Bataan Natural Park) is a protected area spread across the mountainous interior of the northern half of the Bataan Peninsula. It was established on December 1, 1945, under Proclamation No. 24 at about 31,000 hectares; parts were later excluded several times, including about 165 hectares for the Kanawan Negrito reservation under Proclamation No. 192 of 1987, and the area is now commonly given as roughly 23,688 hectares (figures vary by source). The park spans parts of Orani, Abucay, Bagac, Morong, Samal and Hermosa, and Balanga City, and is managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). It lies about
101 km
from Manila in a straight line, is classed as IUCN category II (national park), and is also a BirdLife International Important Bird Area (IBA).
At the center of the park is Mount Natib, a forested, acorn-shaped caldera volcano whose caldera measures roughly 6 km by 7 km. Hiking guides give the summit as about

. Inside the caldera are rivers, springs and waterfalls, with names such as Pasukulan Falls and Dunsulan Falls, and the forest is described as home to wild monkeys, many insects and birds, and flowers and ground orchids. Bataan usually brings to mind war sites and beaches, but what makes this park special is that it is a large tropical forest preserved close to Manila.

There are two main ways travelers use the park. One is the summit climb of Mount Natib, starting from Barangay Tala in Orani, done as a day hike or with a night of camping. The other is a trek that starts from Barangay Gabon in Abucay and walks to the roughly

Pasukulan Falls inside the caldera. Either way the trail is steep, with leeches and mud, so this is not a casual walk, and it is best to hire a guide arranged through the local DENR or tourism office. The Orani route leaves Tala, passes a spot called Pinagbutasan, and follows a wide, rough road across grassland and light woodland before the steep summit push begins from the base camp at the foot of the mountain. The Abucay side is more densely forested with several stream crossings, and the final descent before the falls is on a rope. Some people link the two routes over a day or two, but it is safer to pick one route that suits your fitness and experience.

This guide is based on a 2015 hiking guide, a 2022 trekking account and the park overview on Wikipedia. Registration fees, guide fees and how the jump-offs are run have changed over the years and no official notice was found for many items, so read every price and rule as approximate and check the latest with the DENR Bataan office or the municipal tourism office before you go. In the rainy season, leeches and swollen water raise the risk.

The summit has a small flat area with a DENR signpost. On a clear day the hiking guide says you can see the West Philippine Sea to the west, Mount Mariveles, Mount Samat, Subic Bay, Mounts Cinco Picos and Balingkilat, and Mount Arayat. The climb to the summit takes 3.5–5 hours, and the last section is steep forest and rock.
This waterfall of about
drops on the upper Tiawir River at the southern edge of a smaller caldera east-southeast of the main Natib caldera. Dense foliage hides part of it, and the last
10 minutes
down toward the falls is a steep, roped path. A flat area nearby is used as a campsite.
The trail from Labangan Resort in Barangay Gabon, Abucay, is about
17 km
with a total elevation gain of about
. Waypoints include the DENR shed at Kapehan, the Tanawan View Deck (about 905 m) and an old balete tree. You cross shallow streams several times, and water is available along much of the trail.

The traverse down toward Morong is described as narrow forested ridges and several crossings of the Morong River, ending at the hanging bridge by the Aeta village of Kanawan. It is a harder route, so plan it with an experienced guide.

The park is designated an Important Bird Area, and accounts say wild monkeys, many insects and birds live here. In the forest you meet sounds and signs first, so do not touch or feed animals, and carry out your trash.

The views from the summit and the Tanawan View Deck, and the campsite near Pasukulan Falls inside the caldera, are the highlights of the park. Camping gives you starlight and forest sounds, but be ready for leeches, damp and sudden showers.

2–2.5 hours
From the Orani crossing, take a tricycle to Barangay Tala, register for the climb and find a guide. This takes about
30 minutes
Set off from Tala. After about
1 hour
you pass Pinagbutasan, then continue through grassland and forest, and the summit push begins at the base camp at the foot of the mountain.
At the summit, enjoy the DENR signpost and the views, and have lunch. From the base camp to the summit takes about
90 minutes
Come down the same way. Watch for leeches and wet rock, and aim to finish before dark.
This standard schedule was presented as a one-day trip from Manila, but it varies a lot with fitness and weather, so leave some slack.

Reach Bataan via NLEX and SCTEX, or go around through Pampanga from Manila. Check the exact route on a map app.
The roads to the jump-offs are narrow, so a large vehicle may have to stop at the village entrance and you walk in.
The dry season from November to May is the safe time to visit the park. In the rainy season leeches multiply, streams swell and rocky paths become slippery, which raises the risk.
In March–May, when the midday sun is strong, start early in the morning. In any season showers are frequent on the mountain, so bring waterproof gear and spare clothes.

In November–January, when days are short, the forest darkens quickly if you come down late in the afternoon, so start earlier. The park is too big to see in one day, so on a first visit choose one route and plan the timing with your guide.

There is almost no formal lodging inside the park. Campers use the flat area near Pasukulan Falls or the base camp at the foot of the mountain, and if you plan a single day it is better to stay in Balanga, Orani or Abucay. Ask the DENR or the municipal tourism office in advance about lodging and camping permission.

There are no restaurants on the mountain, so bring packed meals, snacks and plenty of water. Near the jump-offs, small sari-sari stores and wash-up areas are reported. Water is available along much of the Abucay trail, but one account says there is none on the Orani side past the midpoint, so bring a way to purify water.

After the hike, we recommend resting at a restaurant in Balanga for Filipino grilled dishes, seafood and local snacks. The city has lodging, banks and money changers, which makes it a good place to sort out your gear. Check restaurants and prices locally.

Register before going up and hire a guide. There is no fixed price list for guides, so negotiate in advance. A 2015 account listed a DENR contact, but it may have changed, so check with the municipal tourism office first.
There are many leeches, so bring long socks, long trousers, and leech spray or salt. They are especially bad in the rainy season.
Mobile signal is available only at a few points. Prepare offline maps and a power bank.
Grippy hiking boots or trekking shoes are best. The roped sections are optional, but they help in the rainy season.
Bring a headlamp, spare water and energy snacks. The rule is to be down before dark.
Take your trash out and follow Leave No Trace (LNT) principles, without touching wildlife.
If there are beginners in your group, plan a trip only as far as the waterfall instead of the summit.
The paths to Mount Natib and Pasukulan Falls are steep mountain routes with leeches and swollen streams. Do not go in without a guide, and postpone if rain is forecast.
One account mentions meeting snakes. Do not put your hands into grass or rock crevices.
One account says some sections were overgrown and hard to see. Stay with your guide.
The last section just below the summit is steep and rocky and very slippery after rain.
Park rules and fees have changed over the years. The numbers in this guide are old records, so confirm them locally.
Phone signal is available only at a few points such as the Tanawan View Deck and the DENR shed. Tell your lodging or family your plan and expected return time in case you get lost or hurt.
